title: The house fire
hookLine: late in life his house burned, and neighbors rebuilt it while he traveled

cards: Early morning in Concord, and there's smoke coming from the Emerson house.
Neighbors come running, carrying armfuls of books and papers onto the lawn: the manuscripts, the journals, years of a writer's life laid out in the grass. The roof is badly damaged.
The man who wrote Self-Reliance is old now, shaken, and suddenly without a home. What happens next is the part Concord tells and retells. It isn't about Emerson trusting himself.
It's about a whole town deciding not to let him stand alone.

teach.b: First, the rescue. By the usual account, it was neighbors who carried out his books and papers while the house burned. Whatever else was lost, a great deal of his writing survived because other people's arms got it out.

Friends and neighbors gathered money to rebuild the house. They urged Emerson, worn out and unwell, to go away and rest while the work was done. So he traveled abroad, and while he was gone, the town rebuilt his home.
The story goes that when he came back, Concord met him at the station and walked him home, with bells and children and cheering, to a house standing again where the ruin had been.
People who tell it say he was deeply moved. Fourth, the turn it gives this block. For weeks this path has followed Emerson's great theme: stand on your own, trust thyself.
He meant it, and he lived much of it. But the self-reliant man could not rebuild his own roof. His neighbors did.
Read this way, self-trust is a way of thinking, not a plan for living alone. The town didn't argue with his philosophy.
It quietly added the other half: we rely on each other, too.
Some traditions call that charity, some call it community, some call it being a neighbor. Concord simply got to work.

how: In Concord the story of the Emerson house fire is told as a picture of community: neighbors saving his papers, friends paying to rebuild, and the town welcoming him home.

practice: Let your attention move outward, house by house, to someone whose roof, in one way or another, has caught fire lately: a plan, a car, a season of health. Don't solve it in your head.
Just let one face come, and one small, practical thing you could carry for them, the way the neighbors carried the papers out.

wordCard.voice: The house fire. When Emerson's home burned, his neighbors saved his papers, raised money, and rebuilt it while he traveled. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: neighbors rebuild. Even the most self-reliant man in Concord needed a town. Until tomorrow.
